title: One Intercept per Provider
subtitle: the model, as parallel lines
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E04_OneInterceptPerProvider
status: Script approved. Animatic pass built; animation still to come.

segments.visual: The log-odds panel: a vertical log-odds ruler with probability labels, and two positions along the bottom, lower-risk and higher-risk. Two grey dots at the pooled rates, joined by a dashed grey line.

sentences.text: Last time, we pooled all five clinics into a single standard.
Drawn on the log-odds ruler, that standard is one line: lower-risk patients start at 23%, and higher risk is one step up, to 63%.
sentences.say: Drawn on the log-odds ruler, that standard is one line: lower-risk patients start at twenty-three percent, and higher risk is one step up, to sixty-three.

segments.visual: Each clinic's own dots appear in its colour, sized by number of patients. Alder and Dune sit above the line at both ends; Birch and Cedar below at both. Elm's marker rests on the bottom edge with a down arrow: 0 of 11.

sentences.text: Now put the clinics back.
Alder's patients sit above the line, at both ends. So do Dune's.
Birch and Cedar sit below it, at both ends. And Elm, with no readmissions at all, is off the bottom of the chart.

segments.visual: Short vertical ticks mark each miss, in the clinic's colour. The question appears.

sentences.text: One line for everyone misses, and it misses clinic by clinic.
So here is today's question: what is the smallest change that fixes it?

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: one intercept per provider.

segments.visual: Each clinic's two dots are joined by a line of its own. Cedar's carries a small tag: Episode 2.

sentences.text: The obvious fix is to give every clinic a line of its own: its own starting point, and its own step.
That's what we did for Cedar, two episodes ago.

segments.visual: Alder's higher-risk dot pulses: 6 patients. Brackets mark the gap between Alder's and Cedar's lines at each end: 0.69 on the left, 1.20 on the right.

sentences.text: But look at what it costs.
Each line now rests on one clinic's patients alone. Alder's higher-risk end is just 6 people.
sentences.say: Each line now rests on one clinic's patients alone. Alder's higher-risk end is just six people.

sentences.text: And the gap between two clinics is no longer one number. Alder sits further above Cedar for higher-risk patients than for lower-risk ones.

segments.visual: A question mark hangs between the two brackets; the two piles of chips split into four, eight, sixteen.

sentences.text: So the question 'how much higher is Alder?' would have two answers. With a dozen risk factors, it would have thousands.

segments.visual: The four lines pivot until they are parallel. Caption: the bet, one step for everyone.

sentences.text: So let's make a bet instead.
Suppose a risk factor works the same way in every clinic: the same step on the log-odds ruler, wherever you are treated.
Then clinics can differ in only one way: where they start.

segments.visual: A yellow dial labelled beta. Turning it tilts every line together.

sentences.text: Here is that bet as a machine.
One dial, beta, sets the step for everyone. Turn it, and every line tilts together.

segments.visual: One slider per clinic, in its colour, labelled gamma. Moving Alder's slider moves only Alder's line; the tilt does not change.

sentences.text: And every clinic gets a slider of its own. It moves that clinic's line up or down, and leaves the tilt alone.
We'll call that number gamma.

segments.visual: The word intercept labels the left end of a line, at the lower-risk position.

sentences.text: Statisticians call a line's starting point its intercept.
So that's the whole idea: one intercept per provider, and one shared step.

segments.visual: The equation assembles from labels already on screen: log-odds = gamma (clinic) + beta × (higher-risk). Then the compact form, logit(p_ij) = gamma_i + beta·x_ij. Then three yellow steps stack, as in Episode 2.

sentences.text: Written out: a patient's log-odds is their clinic's gamma, plus beta if they are higher-risk.
With more risk factors there are more steps, each with its own beta. There is still just one gamma per clinic.

segments.visual: Name card: the logistic fixed-effect model. Under the word fixed: each gamma is its own unknown number.

sentences.text: This is the logistic fixed-effect model.
'Fixed' means only that each gamma is its own unknown number. We assume nothing about how those numbers are spread across clinics.

segments.visual: The dial and the sliders drift, then settle.

sentences.text: How the dial and the sliders find their best positions is a story for a later episode. For now, here is where they land.

segments.visual: The dial reads beta = 2.02; beside it, odds × 7.5.

sentences.text: The shared step is 2.02.
sentences.say: The shared step is two point zero two.

sentences.text: That is the bet at work: in every clinic, higher risk multiplies the odds of readmission by about seven and a half.

segments.visual: Gamma labels at the left end of each line: Birch −1.82, Cedar −1.52, Alder −0.65, Dune −0.58.

sentences.text: Four sliders settle. Birch is lowest, at minus 1.82. Then Cedar. Then Alder and Dune, close together at the top.
sentences.say: Four sliders settle. Birch is lowest, at minus one point eight two. Then Cedar. Then Alder and Dune, close together at the top.

segments.visual: Elm's line keeps sliding down and leaves the panel. A hatched tag: 0 of 11, no finite gamma.

sentences.text: Elm's never does. With no readmissions at all, a lower line always fits better, so it slides off the chart.
Elm gets an episode of its own.

segments.visual: The ruler switches from log-odds to probability. The lines bend into S-curves of one shape, slid sideways. Markers at the two risk positions: Birch 14% and 55%, Alder 34% and 80%.

sentences.text: Switch to the probability ruler, and the parallel lines become S-curves: one shape, slid sideways.
For a lower-risk patient, the model gives 14% at Birch and 34% at Alder.
sentences.say: For a lower-risk patient, the model gives fourteen percent at Birch and thirty-four at Alder.

sentences.text: For a higher-risk patient, 55% at Birch and 80% at Alder.
sentences.say: For a higher-risk patient, fifty-five percent at Birch and eighty at Alder.

segments.visual: A small tag under the dial: 103 patients, rough estimates.

sentences.text: One caution. With 103 patients, these are rough estimates. How rough is a question for later.
sentences.say: One caution. With a hundred and three patients, these are rough estimates. How rough is a question for later.

segments.visual: The dashed pooled line returns beside the fitted lines: a step of 1.75 against 2.02.

sentences.text: Notice that the step has grown. The pooled line climbed 1.75. These lines climb 2.02.
sentences.say: Notice that the step has grown. The pooled line climbed one point seven five. These lines climb two point zero two.

segments.visual: Inside each clinic, a bracket from its lower-risk dot to its higher-risk dot: Alder 2.30, Birch 1.78, Cedar 1.79, Dune 2.30. Elm has one dot and no bracket.

sentences.text: Here's why. Each clinic is now compared only with itself: its own higher-risk patients against its own lower-risk patients.
Inside Alder, the step is 2.3. Inside Birch, 1.78. Cedar, 1.79. Dune, 2.3.
sentences.say: Inside Alder, the step is two point three. Inside Birch, one point seven eight. Cedar, one point seven nine. Dune, two point three.

segments.visual: The four brackets feed the dial; its needle rests at 2.02. Elm stays dim.

sentences.text: Beta is a compromise among those four, weighted by how much each clinic's patients can tell us.
Elm has no say. All of its patients are lower-risk, so it has no step to offer.

segments.visual: Episode 3's two phrases, how sick and where treated. The where arrows flow into the sliders.

sentences.text: Last time, the pooled rule mixed up how sick patients are with where they were treated.
Now the 'where' has a place of its own: the gammas.
That is the first thing we asked for: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic.

segments.visual: A grey knob labelled beta-zero appears beside the sliders.

sentences.text: You might expect one more number: an overall starting point, with each clinic measured from it.

segments.visual: The grey knob rises by 0.5 while every slider drops by 0.5. The lines and every probability stay exactly where they were. The grey knob is struck out.

sentences.text: Try it. Raise that number by a half, and lower every gamma by a half.
Nothing on screen moves. The data cannot tell those two descriptions apart, so the model keeps only the gammas.

segments.visual: Tags for size, ownership and neighbourhood drop into a clinic's slider and disappear inside it.

sentences.text: The same goes for anything that is identical for every patient at a clinic: its size, its ownership, its neighbourhood.
None of them can have a beta of its own. They are already inside gamma.

segments.visual: Alder's gamma, −0.65, on the log-odds ruler, linked to 34% on the probability ruler. A chip with a 34% slice: a lower-risk patient at Alder.

sentences.text: So what is a gamma? Read it carefully.
Alder's is minus 0.65. That is not a readmission rate. It is a position on the log-odds ruler: the log-odds for a patient with no risk factor switched on.
sentences.say: Alder's is minus zero point six five. That is not a readmission rate. It is a position on the log-odds ruler: the log-odds for a patient with no risk factor switched on.

sentences.text: Here, that's a lower-risk patient at Alder: 34%.
sentences.say: Here, that's a lower-risk patient at Alder: thirty-four percent.

segments.visual: A dozen risk-factor tags, all switched off; the chip fades to an outline.

sentences.text: With many risk factors, that patient may not exist at all. So we will mostly read the gaps between gammas, not the gammas themselves.

segments.visual: Card: gamma is not a pure measure of care. Inside the slider, two parts with no fixed boundary: care, and what we didn't measure about its patients.

sentences.text: And gamma is not a pure measure of care.
It holds everything that is constant within a clinic: how well it looks after patients, but also anything about its patients that we failed to measure. The data cannot separate the two.

segments.visual: Two identical chips, one at Alder and one at Birch, with different slices.

sentences.text: So read a higher gamma this way: for patients who look the same on paper, more readmissions here than there. Why is a separate question.

segments.visual: 200 thin parallel lines. A short scale for the main risk factor's step, with a marker at the truth: 0.80.

sentences.text: Does learning the rule inside providers really help?
Go back to our simulated crowd of 200 providers, where we set the truth ourselves. The true step for the main risk factor is 0.8.
sentences.say: Go back to our simulated crowd of two hundred providers, where we set the truth ourselves. The true step for the main risk factor is zero point eight.

segments.visual: Two more markers on the scale: pooled 0.71, fixed-effect 0.81.

sentences.text: Pool everyone, and the estimate is 0.71, because in this crowd, providers with sicker patients happen to do a little better.
sentences.say: Pool everyone, and the estimate is zero point seven one, because in this crowd, providers with sicker patients happen to do a little better.

sentences.text: Give every provider its own gamma, and the estimate is 0.81.
sentences.say: Give every provider its own gamma, and the estimate is zero point eight one.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Every provider gets its own intercept: gamma.
All providers share one step for each risk factor: beta.
And beta is learned from comparisons inside providers.

segments.visual: Assumption card, three lines: parallel lines (a bet); patients' outcomes independent, given clinic and risk factors; nothing assumed about how the gammas are spread or how they relate to case mix. One dashed line crosses the parallel ones.

sentences.text: Remember what this rests on: the bet that the lines are parallel.
A clinic that does well with lower-risk patients and badly with higher-risk ones would have a line that crosses the others. We will come back and check.

segments.visual: Episode 3's two requirements; the first is ticked. The gammas line up on the log-odds ruler: Elm off the end, then Birch, Cedar, Alder, Dune. Cedar, in the middle, is ringed.

sentences.text: Last time, we asked for two things. The risk rule, we now have.
And the yardstick? Line the gammas up, and one of them sits in the middle: Cedar's.
A middle clinic is a yardstick that no clinic's size can pull toward itself. We'll build on it later.

segments.visual: A bracket between Alder's and Cedar's lines: 0.87. Next episode title.

sentences.text: First, though: Alder's line sits 0.87 above Cedar's. What does that gap mean for an actual patient?
sentences.say: First, though: Alder's line sits zero point eight seven above Cedar's. What does that gap mean for an actual patient?

sentences.text: Next time: reading gamma.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
